body_html:
Tú vs usted is the first decision you make in every Spanish conversation. Both mean “you”, but tú is informal and usted is formal or respectful. Choose well and you sound warm and polite; choose badly and you may sound cold, or overly familiar. The rules vary by country, so in this guide I’ll give you the general principles, the regional differences, and the phrases to switch gracefully.

Quick answer
  • Tú: friends, family, partners, children, people your age in casual settings.
  • Usted: older strangers, formal situations, officials, customers, often your partner’s parents at first.
  • When in doubt, start with usted and let the other person invite you to tú.
  • Plural: vosotros (informal, Spain only) and ustedes (formal in Spain, all uses in Latin America).
{{toc}}

Tú vs usted: the forms

Tú (informal)Usted (formal)
Verb2nd person: tú hablas3rd person: usted habla
Object pronounte: te llamolo / la / le: lo llamo, le digo
Possessivetu casasu casa
Commandpasa, siéntatepase, siéntese
Question¿Cómo estás?¿Cómo está?

Usted comes from the old vuestra merced (“your grace”), which is why it takes third-person verbs. The RAE’s Diccionario panhispánico de dudas explains its forms and agreement.

When to use tú

  • Friends, family members and partners.
  • Children and teenagers.
  • People your age or younger in relaxed settings: parties, classes, gyms, apps.
  • Pets, and God in prayer in most traditions.
  • Most colleagues in modern Spanish workplaces in Spain.

When to use usted

  • Older people you don’t know.
  • Officials, police, doctors, judges.
  • Customers, if you work in a shop, hotel or restaurant.
  • Formal emails and job interviews; see {{link:writing-emails-in-spanish|writing emails in Spanish}}.
  • Often your partner’s parents and grandparents, at least at first; see {{link:talking-to-your-in-laws-in-spanish|talking to in-laws in Spanish}}.
{{image:2}}

Regional differences

RegionTypical habit
SpainTú is very widespread, even with strangers of similar age and in many shops. Usted for the elderly and formal settings.
MexicoMore usted than Spain, especially with older people and in service situations.
Colombia, Costa RicaUsted can be used even between friends, couples and family, as a sign of affection or habit.
Argentina, UruguayVos replaces tú: vos hablás, vos tenés. Usted for formal use.
Central AmericaVos, tú and usted coexist, with local patterns.

I cover more regional variation in {{link:latin-american-vs-spain-spanish|Latin American vs Spain Spanish}}.

Plural: vosotros vs ustedes

In Spain, vosotros is informal plural (¿Qué queréis?) and ustedes formal plural. In Latin America, ustedes is used for every group, formal or not: ¿Qué quieren, chicos? If you learn Latin American Spanish, you can skip vosotros in speaking, though you should recognize it.

{{book:love-slowly}}

How to switch from usted to tú

The switch is usually offered by the older or more senior person:

  • Puedes tutearme. You can call me tú.
  • Háblame de tú, por favor. Please use tú with me.
  • Tutéame, que me haces mayor. Use tú, you’re making me feel old.

You can also ask: ¿Le puedo tutear? or ¿Nos tuteamos? The verb tutear means to address someone as tú; tratar de usted means to use usted.

A quick mental shortcut

Ask yourself: would I call this person by their first name in English, or would I say Mr, Mrs or Dr? First name usually means tú; title usually means usted. Then adjust for the country: more tú in Spain, more usted in Mexico and Colombia.

Why this choice is tricky for learners

Modern English lost its informal “thou” centuries ago, so English gives learners no built-in instinct for this choice. We show respect through titles, tone and word choice instead. In Spanish, the pronoun itself carries the relationship, and it shows up in every verb, pronoun and possessive. The good news is that native speakers know learners find this hard, and almost nobody minds a slip. What matters more is warmth: a smile, por favor and gracias will cover the occasional wrong pronoun. When I translate dialogue, choosing tú or usted for each character is one of the first decisions I make, because it tells the reader so much about who they are to each other.

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
Usted tienes razón.Usted tiene razón.Usted takes third-person verbs
¿Cómo está usted? ¿Y tu familia?¿Cómo está usted? ¿Y su familia?Don’t mix forms
Siéntate, señor.Siéntese, señor.Formal command
Te llamo mañana, doctora.La llamo mañana, doctora.Formal object pronoun

Mixing tú and usted in one sentence is the most common error. Pick one and stay consistent.

{{image:3}}

Try it yourself

Turn these into usted:

  1. ¿Cómo te llamas? → ¿Cómo se llama?
  2. Pasa, por favor. → Pase, por favor.
  3. ¿Quieres un café? → ¿Quiere un café?
  4. Tu pedido está listo. → Su pedido está listo.
  5. Te ayudo. → Le ayudo.

Politeness goes beyond usted; see {{link:spanish-politeness-mistakes|Spanish politeness mistakes}} and {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Start with usted when in doubt, use tú with friends and family, adjust to local habits and stay consistent within a conversation. Nobody will be offended by too much respect, and everyone will appreciate the invitation to tú when it comes.

faq.q: When should I use usted instead of tú?
faq.a: With older people you don’t know, officials, customers, in formal situations and often with your partner’s parents at first. When in doubt, start with usted.
In most countries no, but in Colombia, Costa Rica and some other areas, usted can be used even among friends and family as a habit or sign of affection.

faq.q: What is the difference between vosotros and ustedes?
faq.a: In Spain, vosotros is informal plural and ustedes formal plural. In Latin America, ustedes is used for all groups.
